page_placements.theme: Speculative and parallel decoding efficiency scales conditionally

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper fits scaling relationships for language-model loss using its own model runs, but reports training loss rather than the held-out loss named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The scaling analysis explicitly reports training losses and says no split was held out. The paper does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or architecture invariance. Its downstream benchmark scores are not linked to pretraining loss in a predictive analysis. Table 12 reports fitted losses and model-size hold-out errors; rows below record the loss-scaling findings as related results, not as tests of the held-out-loss versions.
record.test_reason: The paper trains its own AR suite (33.8M–2.77B non-embedding parameters, up to 300B tokens). It fits a Chinchilla-style separable power law to the AR loss with reported fit error and a model-size hold-out error. It fits the same form to a new training regime, the PLM encoder loss. These are its own results on whether loss follows a power law and whether small-run fits predict larger runs. The losses are training losses, but each token is seen roughly once (300B of a 357B-token corpus; losses averaged over the last 200 steps on fresh data), so they approximate held-out loss. That caveat is stated rather than treated as disqualifying.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. Authors conclude that PLM encoder loss tracks an identically trained AR model via an effective model size, so the absolute gap shrinks with scale, while parallelism R grows with size and tokens. They add that their scaling laws predict scaled-up PLMs will reach AR quality while generating many tokens in parallel.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits scaling laws for PLM and autoregressive training losses, rather than reproducing the original held-out-loss measurement or testing a compute-optimal allocation. It uses a Chinchilla-style loss form and reports its own fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted PLM loss depends on the encoder-to-decoder ratio β through the effective parameter count. The paper reports one fitting setup rather than comparing fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Parallelism R (tokens reconstructed per call) follows R ≈ 1 + 1.05 n^0.120 d^0.094 / β^0.16, with fit RMSE 0.024 and 3B hold-out RMSE 0.010.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The decoding parallelism of PLMs grows as a power law in model size and training tokens.

record.code_released: https://github.com/mandt-lab/plm (the paper says the code will be made available)
record.problems: The scaling analysis uses training losses, not held-out losses; Appendix D explicitly says no split was held out. The parameter-count hold-out check is not a held-out data evaluation. The reported coefficient uncertainty is based on delete-one jackknife over only five model sizes.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 and the underlying per-run scaling measurements are not entered as separate rows; the paper fits 104 AR/PLM runs, and the aggregate fitted results and hold-out errors are recorded in R1–R2.

untested.parts: Ranges beyond ~1.9 orders of magnitude in N; a compute-axis fit; a true held-out evaluation split.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude. The hold-outs extrapolate only about 4× (AR, to 1.3B) and 2.6× (PLM, to 3B) in N.
No shape comparison at fixed N.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream scores are not related to scale or loss in any predictive analysis.
No comparison of fitting choices. The exponents (a = 0.194, b = 0.127) differ from Chinchilla's, but the paper does not analyse this.

missing.what: Per-run AR and PLM losses against N at D/N = 90, plotted with the fitted curves
The R scaling law fit and its hold-out error

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'not tested' gate rests on training versus held-out loss. In single-epoch training, the loss on fresh tokens approximates held-out loss, so the verdicts above use the rows with that caveat. The AR law is fitted jointly with the PLM runs. The jackknife uncertainty covers only five sizes. Hyperparameters come from Step Law, which is assumed, not tested. No AR 3B run exists.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits scaling laws to training loss, not held-out pretraining loss.
The 3B/model-size hold-out check concerns training loss, not held-out loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is reported.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training-regime scaling law is tested.
Downstream benchmarks are reported, but the study does not test their predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
The paper reports a particular fitting setup but does not compare fitting choices or test whether they change the exponents or compute-optimal split.

rows.subject: Autoregressive scaling suite (aggregate, 27 runs)
rows.size_stated: 80M, 150M, 350M, 1.3B, and 3B model sizes; no autoregressive 3B run
rows.operation_detail: Fit a joint separable loss law to autoregressive and PLM runs; report the autoregressive loss law and a model-size hold-out check.

conditions.value: training loss; no split held out
For LAR, refit without 1.3B runs and evaluate on the held-out 1.3B autoregressive runs; no autoregressive 3B run

rows.measure: Fitted autoregressive loss scaling law and RMSE
rows.uncertainty: Fitted coefficients: E = 1.105 ± 0.12; A = 0.851 ± 0.11; a = 0.194 ± 0.023; B = 0.763 ± 0.23; b = 0.127 ± 0.032. Uncertainty is delete-one jackknife over five model sizes.
rows.locator: Appendix H, Eqs. (45)–(46) and Table 12; Appendix D, Data
rows.note: n = N/10^8 and d = D/10^10. These are training-loss fits, not held-out-loss results; the paper states that it holds out no data split.
rows.check: Linked to 'none' but it bears on V1 and V2. The AR loss is fitted by L = 1.105 + 0.851/n^0.194 + 0.763/d^0.127 with RMSE 0.0073 across 27 AR runs. Refitting without the 1.3B runs predicts them with RMSE 0.0065. The fit is joint with the PLM runs, not AR-only. Its range is about 1.9 orders of magnitude in N. The loss is single-pass training loss, not a held-out split.

rows.subject: PLM encoder scaling suite (aggregate, 77 PLM runs)
rows.size_stated: 80M, 150M, 350M, 1.3B, and 3B model sizes; the 3B size contributes PLM-β=1 runs only
rows.operation_detail: Fit the PLM encoder loss jointly with the autoregressive loss law, using an effective parameter count dependent on β; report fit and model-size hold-out errors.

conditions.value: training encoder loss; no split held out
Refit without 3B runs and evaluate on 3B runs

rows.measure: Fitted PLM encoder loss scaling law and RMSE
rows.baseline: Autoregressive loss law LAR at the same token count, with effective parameter count neff = Nβ/(β + c)
rows.value: Lenc(N,D,β) = LAR(Nβ/(β + c),D); c = 0.482 ± 0.027; RMSE fit 0.0057, RMSE hold-out 0.0051
rows.uncertainty: c = 0.482 ± 0.027; delete-one jackknife over five model sizes.
rows.locator: Appendix H, Eq. (46) and Table 12; Section 4.1.1
rows.note: The paper describes the PLM encoder as following an identically trained AR model, with the fitted effective-size adjustment. It reports training loss, so this does not establish the held-out-loss claim.
rows.check: Linked to 'none'. PLM encoder loss under a new training objective follows the same separable law via an effective parameter count (c = 0.482), with RMSE 0.0057. Refitting without 3B predicts the 3B PLM-β=1 runs with RMSE 0.0051. The baseline is the AR law, not a control condition. The 'same form' holds only through the fitted effective-size mapping.
